stories.headline: Putin pauses Kyiv strikes before US envoys visit Moscow and Kyiv
stories.dek: Two US envoys met Russian officials in Moscow and are due in Kyiv as Washington tries to restart stalled peace talks.
paragraphs: Russia's president ordered a pause in strikes on Kyiv ahead of a visit by two US envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. They arrived in Moscow to meet Russian officials and are due in Kyiv next. The trip is part of a new US effort to revive peace talks.

The war in Ukraine has dragged on with repeated Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities, including the capital. Earlier peace efforts failed to produce a settlement, and fighting continued. The new shuttle diplomacy puts Washington in direct contact with both sides in close succession, starting in Moscow and then moving to Kyiv.

It is not clear how long the pause will last, whether it covers only Kyiv, or whether attacks will continue elsewhere in Ukraine. Russia has not shown it is ready to accept terms Ukraine can support. The envoys' meetings could reopen talks, but they do not amount to a ceasefire or a deal.
stories.changes: For ordinary readers, this means there may be a brief opening for talks and a short reduction in danger for Kyiv.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean the war is ending, that Russia has stopped fighting, or that any peace agreement is close.

cover.title: Russia halts Kyiv strikes as US envoys visit Moscow
cover.standfirst: President Vladimir Putin ordered a pause in strikes on Kyiv before meetings in Moscow with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. The pair are expected in Kyiv next as Washington tries to restart peace talks. No ceasefire has been announced, and it is unclear how long the pause will last.

art.label: Risograph poster
art.concept: Make the top half a disciplined barrage: identical bright-red missiles slanting down in evenly spaced columns toward a flat federal-blue strip of city at the horizon. Remove exactly one narrow vertical column from the pattern to create a clean corridor, and in that gap place two tiny pale motorcade cars nose-to-tail moving toward Kyiv along a single road; keep the entire lower third empty off-white for cover lines. No extra map detail, no landmarks, no smoke — just the barrage, the missing lane, and the convoy using it.
art.note: Tense and spare; muted reds, slate blue, and winter grey.
art.second_beat: First read: a missile strike pattern; second beat: one column has been deliberately withheld to let the envoys through, so the ‘pause’ feels narrow, tactical, and temporary rather than peaceful.

stories.headline: US disables three Iranian oil tankers after missile attack
stories.dek: Central Command said Iranian missiles targeted a carrier and a destroyer, missed both ships, and drew a strike on tankers near Kharg Island, Jask and Oman.
paragraphs: The United States said it disabled three Iranian oil tankers on Saturday after Iran's Revolutionary Guard fired ballistic missiles at a U.S. aircraft carrier and a destroyer. Central Command said both warships evaded the attack and no Americans were hurt. It called the tanker strikes a direct retaliation.

CENTCOM said the Downy near Kharg Island and the Stark 1 near Jask were permanently disabled. It said the Kylo, sailing empty in the Gulf of Oman, was destroyed after its crew was told to abandon ship. Iranian media reported explosions near Kharg Island and said a tanker was hit.

It is not yet clear how Iran will respond, how much damage the strikes did to oil exports, or whether shipping risks in the Gulf will rise further. At the same time, Western governments are pushing a new nuclear resolution against Iran, while Washington weighs more military steps.
stories.changes: For ordinary readers, this raises the risk of wider conflict in Gulf shipping lanes and could feed into higher energy and transport costs.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean the United States and Iran are in a full declared war, and there is no report here of American casualties or a broad shutdown of Gulf oil traffic.

cover.title: US disables three Iranian oil tankers after missile attack
cover.standfirst: The US military said Iran fired ballistic missiles at an American aircraft carrier and a destroyer in the Persian Gulf on Saturday, but both ships avoided the attack. Washington then struck three Iranian oil tankers near Kharg Island, Jask and the Gulf of Oman. Further retaliation is still unclear.

art.label: Silkscreen
art.concept: A single signal-red stroke enters from the upper left as a ballistic missile arc, aimed toward a dead-black U.S. carrier group held small and unmistakable at upper right: a flat carrier deck with one escort beside it. Just before contact, the red stroke snaps downward into a vertical drop, then continues as a dead ECG flatline across the lower half of the cover, passing through and extinguishing three black tanker silhouettes spaced to read as Kharg Island, Jask, and the Gulf of Oman by their coast shapes alone; keep the bottom third mostly open, with the flatline and tanker hulks low and spare.
art.note: Severe and spare; deep navy, black, rust red, and ash grey.
art.second_beat: First you see a missile miss the carrier; a beat later the same line becomes a stopped heartbeat killing Iran’s three oil tankers instead.

stories.headline: Kremlin uses September vote to ready Russia for wider war
stories.dek: Russia's September regional and local elections are being staged less as a contest than as a tool to build support for more fighting.
paragraphs: Russia will hold regional and local elections from 18 to 20 September, the first such vote since the full invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022. According to Le Monde, the Kremlin is using the ballot not to test public choice but to prepare society for a possible military escalation.

For a newcomer, the key point is that these elections are not described as competitive. The Kremlin tightly manages Russian politics, and voting can serve other purposes besides choosing lawmakers. Here, the vote is presented as part of a broader wartime campaign to rally loyalty, discipline public life, and normalize a longer conflict.

What remains unclear is what form any escalation would take and how far the authorities think public support can be pushed. The summary does not say which regions are voting, what new measures may follow, or whether this political mobilization would lead to more conscription, harsher controls, or both.
stories.changes: For ordinary readers, this suggests Russia's domestic politics are being used more openly to support a longer and possibly harsher war effort.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean a new military step has already happened, or that these September elections will produce a real shift in who governs Russia.

cover.title: Russia uses September elections to build support for war
cover.standfirst: Russia will hold regional and local elections from 18 to 20 September, the first since the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Le Monde reports the Kremlin is treating the vote less as a contest than as a tool to mobilize society for possible military escalation.

art.label: Risograph poster
art.concept: Fill the upper two-thirds with a flat federal-blue silhouette of Russia, cropped large. Carve a clean white void through its interior in the unmistakable shape of a rifle magazine being pushed up into a gun just off the top-right edge; from above, a stream of small fluorescent-pink ballot slips falls into that void and, as they align inside it, they read as rounds feeding the weapon. Keep the lower third mostly empty paper, with only two or three late-falling slips drifting into the type area.
art.note: Severe and controlled; muted red, black, cream, and military green.
art.second_beat: First you see Russia and ballots; a beat later the white space snaps into a gun magazine, making the votes read as ammunition for wider war.

stories.headline: Russian drones hit passenger train bound for Kherson injuring two
stories.dek: The attack came at midday on Saturday as the train was heading toward the southern city of Kherson.
paragraphs: Russian forces attacked a passenger train bound for Kherson with Shahed drones at midday on Saturday, according to Ukrainian reports. Two people were injured. The strike adds to the danger facing civilian travel in southern Ukraine, where routes near the front remain exposed to air attacks.

Kherson is a southern Ukrainian city that has faced repeated Russian attacks since Ukrainian forces retook it in 2022. Shahed drones are explosive drones that Russia uses often against Ukrainian cities and infrastructure. A passenger train is a civilian target, used by ordinary travelers moving between Ukrainian-controlled areas.

It is not yet clear exactly where the train was hit, how serious the injuries were, or whether the train completed its trip. Officials have not yet said how many passengers were on board or whether rail service on the route will change after the attack.
stories.changes: For ordinary passengers in Ukraine, it is another sign that even daytime civilian rail travel near frontline regions can come under attack.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean Ukraine's rail network has stopped running, or that every train to southern cities is now suspended.

cover.title: Russian drones strike passenger train heading to Kherson
cover.standfirst: Russian forces attacked a passenger train bound for Kherson with Shahed drones at midday on Saturday, Ukrainian reports said. Two people were injured. Officials had not yet given the exact location of the strike or said whether the train finished its journey.

art.label: Maximalist doodle
art.concept: A single Ukrainian passenger carriage in strict side view runs across the upper two-thirds of the cover, moving left to right. The left half is ordinary midday travel: repeated train windows, curtains, paired seats, overhead racks, a pram, a thermos, soft bags and jackets; then, at one tearing point near the middle, a Shahed drone slices into the roofline and the right half becomes the instant after impact — roof peeled back, windows blown out, seats twisted, luggage, glass and fabric whipping upward into white space. Keep the lower third largely clear for type by letting the debris arc upward and back, not downward; no background, just the carriage, the tear, and the civilian objects made unmistakable.
art.note: Grave, stark, limited palette of charcoal, faded blue and muted yellow.
art.second_beat: First you see an ordinary passenger coach; a beat later you realize the same carriage has been split in real time from routine travel into violent attack.

stories.headline: Greek air force jet crashes at air show near Athens
stories.dek: A twin-seat Phantom F4 went down during a low pass at Tanagra, where firefighters and aircraft battled the fire.
paragraphs: A Greek air force Phantom F4 crashed during an aerial display at Tanagra air base on Saturday, north of Athens. The jet went down while flying low in front of thousands at the annual Athens Flying Week show. The crash started a large fire, sending black smoke over the base.

Officials said no spectators were hurt. Fire crews kept the blaze away from the crowd while 85 firefighters, 11 water-dropping planes and helicopters worked on the scene. Tanagra air base is about 60 kilometres north of Athens and hosts one of Greece's main public flying events each year.

The main unanswered issue is the fate of the two crew members. Greek air force officials gave no immediate update on their condition. Emergency teams said the fire made access harder on the ground, so a full account of the crash and its cause had not yet been released.
stories.changes: People at the show and nearby now face disruption while officials secure the crash site and investigate what happened.
stories.unchanged: There is no sign of a wider public safety threat beyond the air base, and no spectator injuries were reported.

cover.title: Greek air force jet crashes during air show near Athens
cover.standfirst: A twin-seat Phantom F4 crashed during a low-altitude display at Tanagra air base on Saturday in front of thousands of spectators. No audience injuries were reported. Firefighters, helicopters and water-dropping aircraft fought the blaze as officials tried to reach the two crew members and begin an investigation.

art.label: Gouache painting
art.concept: Paint the scene from the spectator edge of Athens Flying Week: in the quiet lower third, a row of parked family cars and a picnic blanket sit abandoned, with paper plates, bread and plastic cups lightly dusted in soft grey ash. Far beyond them at Tanagra, keep the air base small but unmistakable — runway, low barriers, scrub, and a sideways-drifting wall of black smoke — while two small yellow firefighting aircraft cross through the haze; the crash itself is not shown.
art.note: Hot, smoky, urgent; scorched orange, ash black, dusty blue.
art.second_beat: First you read an ordinary air-show picnic interrupted; a beat later the ash settling on food and windscreens makes the distant Phantom crash feel suddenly intimate and real.

stories.headline: US takes stake in Venezuela oil venture through Pentagon deal
stories.dek: The Pentagon got a free 35% stake in a company with rights to 17 Venezuelan oilfields and broad US control over future output.
paragraphs: The White House disclosed a deal that gives the Pentagon a 35% stake in North American Blue Energy Partners, a private company with century-long rights to 17 Venezuelan oilfields. The administration says the arrangement secures oil for national security and helps pull Venezuela away from Chinese and Russian influence.

This follows the US-backed removal of Nicolás Maduro eight months ago and a new government led by interim president Delcy Rodríguez. Venezuela then granted NABEP access to reserves the White House says total 65 billion barrels. The State Department can buy 20% of output at production cost and gets first refusal on the rest.

The scale of the reserves, the legality of the structure, and the political risk are still unsettled. Historians and trade lawyers say direct US ownership of a foreign oil operator has little precedent. Major US oil companies have mostly stayed away, calling Venezuela too risky after past nationalizations.
stories.changes: It could give the US government a direct hand in foreign oil supply and eventually affect fuel security and public exposure to overseas energy deals.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean the US government will run Venezuelan oilfields day to day or that gasoline prices will change soon.

cover.title: US takes direct stake in Venezuelan oil venture
cover.standfirst: The Pentagon received a free 35% stake in a Barbados-based oil company with rights to 17 Venezuelan fields for 100 years. The US can also buy part of the oil at production cost and block key board choices, while legal and political challenges remain unresolved.

art.label: Punk cutout
art.concept: On a flat hazard-orange ground, show a brutal black silhouette where the Pentagon itself has become an oil pumpjack: the five-sided building is the machine body, unmistakable in plan and mass, with a single long pump arm caught mid-downstroke. Directly beneath the arm, a stark white puddle in the exact shape of Venezuela is being struck and drained, with just a few black drops and one rough slashing marker stroke to drive the motion downward; keep the lower third largely open for type.
art.note: Hard-edged and uneasy; black, rust, cream, and dark red.
art.second_beat: First you see a pumpjack; a beat later you realize the pump is the Pentagon itself, actively extracting oil from Venezuela.

stories.headline: Philippines vice president posts bail after arrest order
stories.dek: Sara Duterte paid 360,000 pesos bail on three grave threat charges tied to remarks about President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
paragraphs: Philippines Vice President Sara Duterte posted bail on Saturday after a court ordered her arrest a day earlier. She faces three counts of grave threats over remarks prosecutors say targeted President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., his wife and a senior lawmaker. Her lawyers say she will fight the case.

The charges come from a 2024 online news conference where Duterte said an assassin should kill Marcos, his wife and then-House Speaker Martin Romualdez if she were killed. She later said she was speaking about her own safety. The case sits inside a wider break between the Marcos and Duterte families.

It is not yet clear how fast the criminal case will move or whether it will damage Duterte's path to the 2028 presidential race. She also faces a separate Senate impeachment trial. A conviction could bar her from public office, but she denies wrongdoing and remains vice president for now.
stories.changes: The case raises the legal and political risk for a sitting vice president who could otherwise run for president in 2028.
stories.unchanged: This does not remove Sara Duterte from office today, and it does not settle the separate impeachment case against her.

cover.title: Philippines vice president posts bail after threat case arrest order
cover.standfirst: Sara Duterte posted 360,000 pesos bail in Manila on Saturday after a court ordered her arrest over alleged threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., his wife and a senior lawmaker. She denies the charges. The criminal case and her Senate impeachment trial will now move ahead in parallel.

art.label: Object photograph
art.concept: On a pale green seamless background, show the metal slot and teeth of a courtroom-style evidence shredder low in frame, with a small, unmistakable fan of real Philippine 1,000-peso notes caught halfway into the mouth mid-feed. Keep everything else out: no hands, no extra props, just the cash being actively swallowed by the machine, with the lower third left clean for type and the notes angled so their Philippine look reads by color, portrait layout and security-mark pattern rather than any legible text.
art.note: Tense and procedural; red, black and off-white.
art.second_beat: First you see bail money; a beat later you realise it is not paying freedom so much as being consumed by the legal process itself.

stories.headline: US employers added 162,000 jobs in August, far above forecasts
stories.dek: The Labor Department also revised June and July upward, while unemployment held at 4.1% and manufacturing posted its strongest month since 2023.
paragraphs: The U.S. economy added 162,000 nonfarm jobs in August, well above the 53,000 economists had expected. The Labor Department also raised its estimates for June and July by a combined 55,000 jobs. The report matters now because it suggests hiring was stronger than recent weak readings had implied.

Nonfarm payrolls are the government’s main monthly count of jobs across the economy, excluding farm work. August’s gain was the strongest since March. Manufacturing added 16,000 jobs, its best month since late 2023. The unemployment rate stayed at 4.1% even as labor force participation rose to 61.6%.

One month does not settle the question of where the labor market is heading. Hiring had averaged only 31,000 jobs a month over the previous year, so August could prove temporary. It is also not clear yet whether stronger payroll growth will affect Federal Reserve thinking on interest rates or inflation risks.
stories.changes: For an ordinary reader, this points to a job market that may be sturdier than feared, especially if you are looking for work in manufacturing or other large employers.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean the economy is suddenly booming, wages are guaranteed to rise, or that one strong month removes the risk of slower growth later this year.

cover.title: US economy added 162,000 jobs in August
cover.standfirst: The Labor Department said employers added 162,000 nonfarm jobs in August, far above forecasts of 53,000. June and July were revised up by 55,000 jobs combined. Unemployment held at 4.1% as more people entered the workforce. Investors and policymakers will now watch to see if the strength lasts.

art.label: Drawn chart
art.concept: A hand-drawn bar chart climbs across the upper two-thirds of the cover, with all earlier months as flat dark bars and the final August bar the only accent colour, clearly the tallest. Perched on top of that bar is a simple factory time-card rack, and a cluster of punched cards is caught mid-drop into its slots, so the bar is visibly still being added to; keep the lower third empty and quiet for type.
art.note: Crisp, factual mood; navy, gray, and muted red on off-white.
art.second_beat: First you see a jobs bar surging; a beat later you realise the surge is literally payroll being added, and specifically factory payroll.

stories.headline: Pogacar ends season after Vuelta crash left him with neck fracture
stories.dek: The Tour de France champion will miss the World Championships after surgery on a broken collarbone, concussion and a stable neck fracture.
paragraphs: Tadej Pogacar will not race again this season because of injuries from his crash at the Vuelta a Espana last month. His team announced the decision now after assessing his recovery from surgery on a broken collarbone, a concussion, a stable neck fracture and multiple abrasions.

Pogacar, 27, is one of road cycling's biggest riders and a five-time Tour de France champion. He crashed on stage eight while leading the Vuelta and dropped out of the race. He had hoped to win the Vuelta for the first time and complete victories in all three Grand Tours.

He will now miss the World Championships in Montreal, where he was due to defend his rainbow jersey, plus the European Championships in Ljubljana and Il Lombardia. It is not clear when he will race again, though his team said it will not rush his return and he has extended his contract until 2032.
stories.changes: Fans will not see Pogacar at the biggest late-season races, including the World Championships and Il Lombardia.
stories.unchanged: This does not end his career; his team says the pause is to let him recover fully, and he remains under contract for years.

cover.title: Tadej Pogacar will miss the rest of the season
cover.standfirst: Tadej Pogacar will not race again this year after his Vuelta a Espana crash left him with a broken collarbone, concussion and a stable neck fracture. The 27-year-old Slovenian will miss the World Championships in Montreal later this month, while his team says his return will not be rushed.

art.label: Comic absurd
art.concept: A winner’s podium is shown in one clean side-on view, split by transformation rather than a literal line: at left, the top step is still a victory dais with a rainbow jersey draped over it and flash-burst cameras crowding low in the foreground; as the form moves right, the podium buckles and lengthens into a hospital trolley being wheeled away, with the top step becoming a rigid white neck brace and a sling in one continuous shape. Keep the right side sparse and clinical, with just the trolley wheels lifting into motion and a single blank hospital wristband looped from the rail; leave the lower third largely open for type.
art.note: Quiet, bruised mood; late-summer colors with muted reds, road gray and washed rainbow bands.
art.second_beat: First you read triumph turning into medical exit; a beat later, you see the podium’s top step has become the neck brace itself, making the season-ending injury feel like the victory structure collapsing into treatment.

stories.headline: Hong Kong astronaut will teach students in live lesson from orbit
stories.dek: Lai Ka-ying and two Shenzhou-23 crewmates will answer questions and show space experiments to students in Hong Kong and Macau.
paragraphs: Hong Kong said its first astronaut, Lai Ka-ying, will soon give a live lesson from China’s space station with her two Shenzhou-23 crewmates. The class is aimed at students and teachers in Hong Kong and Macau. Officials announced the plan on Saturday but did not give a date or time.

The event is part of the Tiangong Class programme run with the China Manned Space Agency. It will include an expert talk, science demonstrations in orbit and a question-and-answer session. Hong Kong schools will watch on campus, while Macau will send a visiting group to attend in the city.

Key details are still missing. Officials have not said when the broadcast will happen, how long it will last or which schools will take part in person. It is also not clear what experiments the crew will show. The lesson will also be streamed online and carried by local television stations.
stories.changes: Students in Hong Kong and Macau will get a direct view of life and science experiments aboard China’s space station.
stories.unchanged: This is a teaching event, not a change to space policy, school exams or public access to the astronaut programme.

cover.title: Hong Kong astronaut will give students a live lesson from space
cover.standfirst: Hong Kong said Lai Ka-ying, the city’s first astronaut, will soon join two Shenzhou-23 crewmates in a live Tiangong Class for students and teachers in Hong Kong and Macau. The broadcast will include space experiments and questions from students, but officials have not yet released the date or time.

art.label: Decorative flat
art.concept: Show a Hong Kong classroom blackboard as a large dark rectangle dominating the cover, but inside its bounds is the rounded interior of the Tiangong station in decorative flat cutaway: curved white handrails, soft experiment pouches, a circular hatch, and a few droplets and paper-star shapes drifting upward in zero gravity. Along the very bottom edge, keep a thin quiet strip for type and place only a tiny row of students at desks looking up, so the blackboard reads first as a school object and then as an impossible live portal where the lesson is already happening.
art.note: Bright, calm, educational mood; deep blue, white and soft silver palette
art.second_beat: First you see a classroom blackboard; a beat later you realise the blackboard contains the space station itself, making the students below feel suddenly small and the lesson vividly live from orbit.
